description: Experience the irresistible crunch of authentic Japanese Karaage, a beloved dish featuring perfectly seasoned, bite-sized chicken pieces. Each morsel is incredibly juicy on the inside with a delicate, super crispy exterior, thanks to a unique double-frying technique. This recipe brings the taste of Japan's best fried chicken right to your home kitchen.

instructions.title: Prepare the Chicken
instructions.text: Cut the boneless, skin-on chicken thighs into roughly 1.5-inch bite-sized pieces. Pat them dry with paper towels to ensure better marinade absorption.

instructions.title: Marinate the Chicken
instructions.text: In a large bowl, combine the soy sauce, sake, mirin, grated ginger, grated garlic, sesame oil, and black pepper. Add the chicken pieces and mix well to coat thoroughly. Cover the bowl and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes, or preferably 1-2 hours for deeper flavor.

instructions.title: Coat the Chicken
instructions.text: After marinating, crack the egg into the bowl with the chicken and mix well. Then, add the potato starch (or cornstarch) gradually, mixing until each piece of chicken is evenly coated and no dry spots of starch remain.

instructions.title: First Fry
instructions.text: Heat about 4 cups of frying oil in a deep pot or Dutch oven to 340°F (170°C). Carefully drop chicken pieces into the hot oil, making sure not to overcrowd the pot. Fry for 2-3 minutes until lightly golden and cooked through. Remove and drain on a wire rack.

instructions.title: Rest the Chicken
instructions.text: Allow the first-fried chicken pieces to rest for at least 5-10 minutes. This resting period helps redistribute moisture and prepares them for the second fry, ensuring maximum crispiness.

instructions.title: Second Fry for Crispiness
instructions.text: Increase the oil temperature to 375°F (190°C). Return the chicken pieces to the hot oil, frying in batches for another 1-2 minutes until they are deep golden brown and exceptionally crispy.

instructions.title: Serve Immediately
instructions.text: Remove the crispy Karaage from the oil and drain on a wire rack or paper towels. Serve hot with a squeeze of fresh lemon, a side of Japanese mayonnaise, or your favorite dipping sauce.

tips: For the crispiest Karaage, do not skip the double-frying step. The first fry cooks the chicken, and the second fry at a higher temperature creates that signature crunch.
Using potato starch is key to achieving the light, airy, and incredibly crispy coating characteristic of authentic Karaage. Cornstarch is a good substitute if potato starch is unavailable.
Serve Karaage immediately after the second fry for the best texture. It pairs wonderfully with fresh lemon wedges, Japanese mayonnaise, or a sprinkle of shichimi togarashi for extra flavor.
article:
Mastering Karaage: The Ultimate Crispy Japanese Fried Chicken

Japanese cuisine offers a world of exquisite flavors, and among its many culinary jewels, Karaage stands out. Often hailed as the ultimate crispy Japanese fried chicken, Karaage (pronounced kah-rah-ah-geh) is a beloved staple in Japan, from izakayas to bento boxes. It's a meticulously marinated, perfectly coated, and expertly fried delight, promising a burst of umami with every bite. If you're searching for the ultimate Karaage recipe to bring authentic Japanese taste to your table, you've come to the right place. Get ready to transform humble chicken thighs into golden-brown, juicy perfection.

## What is Karaage?
Karaage is a Japanese cooking technique where ingredients, most commonly chicken, are lightly coated and deep-fried. Chicken Karaage is iconic, distinguished by its unique marinade: a blend of soy sauce, sake, mirin, ginger, and garlic, infusing deep, savory flavors. The coating, typically potato starch (katakuriko), creates an incredibly light and airy crispness, unlike heavier Western fried chicken crusts. The result is consistently juicy meat encased in a delicate, shatteringly crisp exterior – a true testament to elegant Japanese cooking.

## Ingredients for the Best Karaage
Crafting perfect Karaage begins with quality ingredients. This Karaage recipe prioritizes freshness and authentic Japanese staples.
